 How video games made me an artist
 By Avalon Kail 
 • 
 October 27, 2026 
 Ashley La 
 I always wanted to be someone who could sit down and make art. If I sat down with a canvas and a paintbrush, I’d be tormented by an overload of ideas and end up with a solid block of color. I’ve never sewn a stitch in my life, plagued by the permanence of altering clothing. I pawn my too-big shirts and too-long jeans off to someone who can sew, seething in jealousy that I can’t do it myself.  
 Despite believing that most were mind-numbing, I found a creative outlet in video games. Having specific requirements tricked my structured brain into using artistry to meet my objective. My clients in Dressmaker need dresses for specific events, and I have to use the drawing tool in Tomodachi Life if I want my fictional characters to look accurate. I live a double life as a medieval seamstress and pixel artist without realizing I’m creating works of art. 
 Dressmaker debuted in September, created by Jonathan Hau-Yoon. The extensively detailed mechanics mimic the real process of dressmaking, complete with fabrics, designs, accessories and a sewing machine. Eccentric characters come to your shop with specific criteria your creation must meet, unless you indulge in crafting your own “off-the-rack” dresses.  
 Hau-Yoon developed Dressmaker for his wife, Sabrina Becker. Becker’s Ehlers-Danlos syndrome — a connective tissue disorder — made it difficult to design clothing with real materials. Hau-Yoon sought to invent a game that perfectly replicated dressmaking from scratch so his wife wouldn’t have to give up what she loved.  
 Any combination of medieval-style bodices, collars, sleeves and skirts resides in an ornamental sketchbook. After taking clients’ measurements and cutting out patterns using one of the 450 fabrics — a tedious puzzle if you’re like me and desperately squeeze your cutouts together to save on fabric — you stitch the segments together with a sewing machine powered by your spacebar.  
 As a rules-conscious player, the innovation of choosing different fabrics satisfied my creativity, even with relatively low effort. But I had been skipping the step so many players had maximized: the accessories. My entire algorithm since the game’s release has been curated murals across flouncy skirts using only the ribbon tool.  
 “A lot of our players make whole paintings on the dresses, using the trims and buttons and things,” Becker said to The Guardian . “They’re drawing Starry Night and the Sistine Chapel.”  
 I’ve been craving a creative outlet in the form of a game since I lost the motivation to continue Tomodachi Life on my Nintendo Switch. That game felt more like painting to me, since the new drawing tool in Mii creation was essential. I mastered the use of my pointer finger and small pixels to make facial features and accessories. The mirror tool and undo button were my saviors while learning the mechanics, and some Miis I spent hours drawing never even made it onto my island.  
 It was shocking to me that gaming could look like this and that there are genres other than shooters and racing games. The game’s objective being drawing and designing made it less daunting, so I could avoid the bogged-down feeling my perfectionism usually brings. Having a starting point cured the blocks in my brain. After searching for Tomodachi Life tutorials and Dressmaker hacks on social media, my brainrotted feed is often interrupted with breathtaking digital art. Through these 30-second clips, I can feel the resurgence of artistry in a generation desperate for expression.  
 These games have made art accessible and far less intimidating to me, and the creativity of others inspires me to get off my phone. My screen time on TikTok dwindles while I rack up my hours on Dressmaker.
